claims.text: The baseline material is a W–Cu composite containing uncoated tungsten particles embedded in a copper matrix.
Applying a conformal copper coating to tungsten particles enhances copper-network connectivity at W–Cu interfaces after consolidation.
An enhanced copper network at W–Cu interfaces reduces interfacial thermal resistance.
Improved continuity of the copper phase facilitates more effective phonon and electron transport.
Reduced W–Cu interfacial thermal resistance increases the overall thermal conductivity of the composite.
A tungsten core confers mechanical strength or durability to the composite.
A tungsten core confers irradiation resilience to the composite.
The copper coating does not compromise the mechanically and irradiation-relevant properties of the tungsten core.
The coated-particle composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise identically processed composite made with uncoated tungsten particles.
The coated-particle composite will maintain mechanical durability similar to that of the uncoated-particle control.
The coated-particle composite will maintain irradiation resistance similar to that of the uncoated-particle control.
The proposed benefit should persist at temperatures and irradiation doses typical of fusion-reactor joint applications if the coating remains intact.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity improvement depends on copper-coating uniformity and thickness.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant thermal-conductivity increase, exemplified as greater than 5%, or any degradation of mechanical durability or irradiation resistance would falsify the hypothesis.
